To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
early-life carotenoid access affected adult immune responses, but did not affect adult carotenoid levels or beak color.

developmental and adult diet did not affect beak coloration in adult mallards, but that individuals that received low-carotonoid diets during development had larger cutaneous immune responses to an immune challenge at adulthood, and that strong cutaneous immune responses were correlated with decreases in beak coloration.

(1) developmental access to carotenoids affected adult circulating carotenoids and PHA response, but did not affect adult immune responses, beak color, or other measures of immune function; (2) early-life access to carotenoid-poor diets resulted in higher circulating carotenoids during an immune challenge; and (3) beak coloration was positively correlated with PHA response, which in turn was associated with losses in caratenoid-pigmented plumage coloration.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of early-life access to carotenoids on adult immune function depend on the immune challenge used, but that these effects are not necessarily linked to beak pigmentation.
early-life access to carotenoids may have lasting impacts on immune function, and that the effects of early-life carotenoid access on immune function may depend on the quality of the adult diet.
the effects of developmental plasticity are not always predictable and may be context dependent, and that developmental plasticity may not necessarily be adaptive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of diet on immune function are likely context-specific, and that the effects of early-life access to nutrients can persist into adulthood.

the effects of developmental conditions on adult phenotype can be complex, and that a variety of mechanisms may be involved in the expression of phenotypes that are tuned to environmental conditions experienced early in life.
